This worksheet analyses data from three experiments: a training programme
(two groups), three ways of communicating (three groups), and a website A/B
test. It has two kinds of sections:

- 👀 **Together** — the code is complete. Run each chunk while we go through
  it in class, and read the comments.
- ✍️ **Your turn** — fill in the blanks `____`. Every task is a near-copy of
  the *Together* chunk just before it: look there first. Each task ends with
  a short check of your result.

⭐ marks tasks for the fast ones; if you run out of time, skip them — the
solutions published after the session cover everything.

**Tip:** render the document now and then. Blanks you have not filled in yet
show up as errors, but the rest of the document still renders.

# Setup 👀

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(effectsize)   # cohens_d(), eta_squared()
library(car)          # leveneTest()

leadership    <- read.csv("data/leadership_study_between.csv")
communication <- read.csv("data/communication_study.csv")
ab_test       <- read.csv("data/exercise_data.csv")
```

---

# Part 1: Comparing two groups

## 1.1 Does leadership training improve team performance? 👀

60 teams, randomly assigned: 30 to a training programme, 30 to a control
group.

```{r}
#| label: leadership-plot

ggplot(leadership, aes(x = group, y = team_performance)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "red")
```

```{r}
#| label: leadership-assumptions

# Normal within each group? (H0: normal)
leadership |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(team_performance)$p.value)

# Equal variances? (H0: equal)
leveneTest(team_performance ~ factor(group), data = leadership)
```

```{r}
#| label: leadership-test

# Both p-values above 0.05: the classic t-test with equal variances
t.test(team_performance ~ group, data = leadership, var.equal = TRUE)

# Effect size: the difference in standard deviations
cohens_d(team_performance ~ group, data = leadership)
```

## 1.2 Your turn ✍️ — the A/B test

100 website visitors, randomly shown a `Simple` or a `Complex` design. Does
the design change the time spent on the site (`time_on_site`, seconds)?

**a.** Copy of the plot in 1.1.

```{r}
#| label: ab-plot

ggplot(ab_test, aes(x = ____, y = ____)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "red")
```

**b.** Are the variances equal?

```{r}
#| label: ab-levene

leveneTest(____ ~ factor(design), data = ab_test)
```

**c.** If Levene's p-value is *below* 0.05, the variances differ: use
Welch's t-test, which is what `t.test()` does when you leave out
`var.equal = TRUE`.

```{r}
#| label: ab-test

t.test(time_on_site ~ ____, data = ab_test)
cohens_d(time_on_site ~ design, data = ____)
```

*Check:* the complex design should come out with the longer mean time.

**Your answers:**

- Levene's p-value: _______ → equal variances? _______
- Mean time: Complex _______ s, Simple _______ s; p-value _______
- Cohen's d = _______ — a _______ effect (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large)

# Part 2: Comparing three or more groups

## 2.1 Which communication method satisfies most? 👀

90 participants, randomly assigned to email, video call or face-to-face.

```{r}
#| label: comm-plot

ggplot(communication, aes(x = communication_method, y = satisfaction_score)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "red")
```

```{r}
#| label: comm-anova

anova_model <- aov(satisfaction_score ~ communication_method, data = communication)
summary(anova_model)   # is at least one group different?
```

ANOVA is a regression with a categorical variable — same F, same p-value:

```{r}
#| label: comm-lm

lm_model <- lm(satisfaction_score ~ communication_method, data = communication)
anova(lm_model)
coef(lm_model)   # intercept = mean of the reference group ("email", first alphabetically)
```

## 2.2 Your turn ✍️ — effect size, post-hoc tests, reference group

**a.** How much of the variance does the method explain? (Copy of
`cohens_d()`, for ANOVA.)

```{r}
#| label: comm-eta

eta_squared(____)
```

**b.** Which groups differ? Tukey's test compares all pairs and corrects for
multiple testing.

```{r}
#| label: comm-tukey

TukeyHSD(____)
```

**c.** Make face-to-face the reference group, as in lab 10: turn the
variable into a factor, then `relevel()`.

```{r}
#| label: comm-relevel

communication_f2f <- communication |>
  mutate(communication_method = relevel(factor(communication_method), ref = "____"))
coef(lm(satisfaction_score ~ communication_method, data = communication_f2f))
```

*Check:* in **c**, the intercept is the mean of the face-to-face group, and
the two other coefficients are differences to it.

**Your answers:**

- η² = _______ → the method explains _______ % of the variance in satisfaction
- Pairs that differ significantly: _______; pair that does not: _______
- Email vs face-to-face: _______ points

# Part 3: How many participants do you need?

## 3.1 Power analysis 👀

Before an experiment: how many participants per group do we need to detect
an effect of a given size with, say, 80 % probability (*power*)? Base R does
this for t-tests.

```{r}
#| label: power-n

# Leadership study: a difference of 9 points, standard deviation 9 (d = 1)
power.t.test(delta = 9, sd = 9, power = 0.80)   # → n per group
```

```{r}
#| label: power-power

# The other way round: with 30 per group, how much power did the study have?
power.t.test(n = 30, delta = 9, sd = 9)
```

## 3.2 Your turn ✍️ — a small effect

Most effects in management research are small. Set `sd = 1`; then `delta`
is Cohen's d directly.

**a.** How many participants per group for d = 0.3 and 80 % power?

```{r}
#| label: power-small

power.t.test(delta = ____, sd = 1, power = 0.80)
```

**b.** ⭐ And for 90 % power? And how much power would 30 per group give for
d = 0.3?

```{r}
#| label: power-small-2

power.t.test(delta = 0.3, sd = 1, power = ____)
power.t.test(n = ____, delta = 0.3, sd = 1)
```

*Check:* the answer in **a** is in the hundreds, not in the tens.

**Your answers:** n per group for d = 0.3: _______ (80 %), _______ (90 %);
power with 30 per group: _______
